props.title: The Shop Around the Corner
props.initialSlug: Two rival shop clerks unknowingly fall in love by mail

sections.content: The Shop Around the Corner represents Ernst Lubitsch's masterful touch at its finest, setting the template for romantic comedies about antagonistic couples who don't realize they're falling in love. Jimmy Stewart and Margaret Sullavan spark as feuding shop employees unknowingly exchanging romantic letters - a plot device that influenced everything from You've Got Mail (1998) to modern dating app rom-coms. Lubitsch transforms a Budapest leather goods shop into a microcosm of human relationships, using his signature wit and sophisticated humor to explore workplace dynamics, class differences, and the gap between public faces and private hearts.

movies.title: Little Shop of Horrors
movies.slug: While not directly related, another beloved shop-centered film mixing romance, comedy and horror

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond its direct remakes. Its DNA can be found in workplace romances like The Proposal (2009) and Two Weeks Notice (2002), where professional antagonism masks growing attraction. The theme of anonymous correspondence leading to love appears in Dear John (2010) and 84 Charing Cross Road (1987), though few match Lubitsch's delicate balance of comedy and poignant human observation.

Lubitsch's direction pioneered techniques still used in romantic comedies today - the careful pacing of revelations, the use of dramatic irony, and what became known as "the Lubitsch touch" - a sophisticated blend of wit, emotion and innuendo. His influence can be seen in films like Sleepless in Seattle (1993) and When Harry Met Sally (1989), which similarly explore how people can be simultaneously perfect for and completely wrong for each other. SUBHEAD: The Legacy of Workplace Romance Films

movies.title: She Loves Me
movies.slug: Broadway musical adaptation of the same source material, capturing the romantic comedy elements

sections.content: While The Shop Around the Corner set the standard for workplace romance, later films like Working Girl (1988) and Nine to Five (1980) expanded the genre to examine power dynamics and gender politics. The confined setting of a workplace creates natural tension and forced proximity, a device used effectively in modern films like Set It Up (2018) and Long Shot (2019). The shop setting itself becomes almost another character, much like in later films such as Empire Records (1995) or High Fidelity (2000).
